title: David Crowley sued Milwaukee Police Department, leading to $1.9 million city settlement
text:
David Crowley sued Milwaukee Police Department, leading to $1.9 million city settlement
L. Y. Vega
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley sued the Milwaukee Police Department, accusing its officers of racism, according to an Aug. 19 report. The lawsuit, which included Crowley and five other plaintiffs, resulted in a $1.9 million payment from the city for attorney’s fees and litigation costs.
The case led to a settlement known as the Collins Agreement. Officers have said this agreement has limited their ability to conduct proactive policing in Milwaukee and contributed to increases in reckless driving and crime rates. After implementation of the Collins Agreement, both traffic stops and field interviews by police declined sharply.
In 2017, when Crowley was a state Assembly member, he joined the American Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit against the department as a plaintiff. The ACLU alleged that Milwaukee police were conducting unconstitutional stop-and-frisk operations targeting Black residents based on racial profiling. The organization wrote: “The revised complaint adds three named plaintiffs to the lawsuit, one of whom is Representative David Crowley... Like the other named plaintiffs and tens of thousands of other Milwaukeeans of color, Rep. Crowley has been subject to an unconstitutional stop and frisk by the Milwaukee police without reasonable suspicion of criminal activity and based on racial profiling.”
Milwaukee Police Chief Jeffrey Norman called for significant changes to the Collins Agreement in 2025 during a panel discussion. Norman said, “I absolutely do believe that the Collins agreement should be modified. It should be heavily modified.” He described it as creating “a cumbersome, burdensome administrative process that does hurt proactive policing.” According to Norman, requirements such as documenting every stop or frisk have discouraged officers from making stops due to increased paperwork demands.
Statistics reported since implementation show that field interviews conducted by officers decreased 90% since 2017; compared with 2012 figures before media scrutiny intensified around accusations of racial bias within MPD practices—field interviews dropped from over 71,000 annually in 2012 to just 41 in December 2022, while traffic stops decreased by nearly four-fifths since the ACLU lawsuit.
summary: The lawsuit, which included Crowley and five other plaintiffs, resulted in a $1.9 million payment from the city for attorney’s fees and litigation costs. Officers have said this agreement has limited their ability to conduct proactive policing in Milwaukee and contributed to increases in reckless driving and crime rates. The ACLU alleged that Milwaukee police were conducting unconstitutional stop-and-frisk operations targeting Black residents based on racial profiling.
